chapter_title: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
learning_objective: The learner will compare predicted retention under massed, evenly spaced, and expanding review schedules, each done by rereading or by retrieval, and correctly predict which schedule and method retain the most on a day-30 exam.
specification:
Type: chart **sim-id:** spacing-retrieval-retention-explorer
**Library:** Chart.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** compare
**Learning Objective:** The learner will compare predicted retention under massed, evenly spaced, and expanding review schedules, each done by rereading or by retrieval, and correctly predict which schedule and method retain the most on a day-30 exam. **Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-sciences/tree/main/docs/sims/spaced-retrieval-timeline
**Prerequisites:** learning versus performance, forgetting curve, spaced practice, massed practice, retrieval practice, desirable difficulty (all defined in the sections "Education and Learning" and "Spaced Practice and Retrieval Practice" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** Before any curve is shown, the learner makes two committed predictions: (P1) which of the four schedules gives the highest day-30 retention — correct answer "Expanding"; (P2) which method, reread or retrieval, gives higher day-30 retention for the same schedule — correct answer "Retrieval." A third check (P3) asks, after the learner has viewed the exam-day options, which schedule gives the highest retention on a day-1 exam — correct answer "Massed." Mastery is 3 of 3. Switching schedules and exam days after the predictions is exploration. **Misconceptions:** (1) Cramming is efficient because it gives the best score on tomorrow's test, so it must be the best way to learn. (2) Rereading is as good as testing yourself. (3) The total time spent studying is what matters, not when it happens. **Instructional Rationale:** Understanding a comparison is strongest when the learner first commits to a prediction that may be wrong and then sees the curves. Including a day-1 exam option lets the learner discover why cramming feels effective while still failing at day 30. **Content:** Four schedules (review times in days after the first lesson at day 0): | Schedule | Review times (days) | |---|---| | No review | none | | Massed | 0.042, 0.083, 0.125 (1, 2 and 3 hours after the lesson) | | Evenly spaced | 1, 3, 7 | | Expanding | 1, 4, 12 | Two methods: Reread, Retrieval. Three exam days: 1, 7, 30. Predicted retention at the exam (model values, rounded to whole percents), used to check the sim: | Schedule | Exam day 1, Reread | Exam day 1, Retrieval | Exam day 7, Reread | Exam day 7, Retrieval | Exam day 30, Reread | Exam day 30, Retrieval | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | No review | 72% | 72% | 10% | 10% | 0% | 0% | | Massed | 76% | 78% | 12% | 14% | 0% | 0% | | Evenly spaced | 72% | 72% | 60% | 74% | 20% | 43% | | Expanding | 72% | 72% | 72% | 83% | 40% | 65% | **Provenance:** The model is illustrative, written for this chapter to show the direction of effects reported by Ebbinghaus (1885), Cepeda et al. (2006), and Roediger and Karpicke (2006). Its numbers are not measured data, and the sim must label every curve "Illustrative model, not experimental data." **Rules:** Retention R(t) = exp(−(t − t_last) / S), where t is days since the first lesson, t_last is the time of the most recent review (0 at the start), and S is memory stability in days. Initial S = 3 days. At each review at time t, compute R at that moment, then update S_new = S × (1 + k × (1 − R)), with k = 2 for Reread and k = 4 for Retrieval, and set t_last = t. A review whose time is greater than or equal to the exam day is skipped. Retention is shown as a percent rounded to the nearest whole number. The curve is plotted from day 0 to the selected exam day. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner makes predictions P1 and P2 and submits them. Nothing is plotted before submission. 2. The sim plots the four schedules for the Reread method, exam day 30, and marks the day-30 retention of each. 3. The learner switches the method to Retrieval. The four curves update; the Reread curves remain visible as faint references for comparison. 4. The learner switches the exam day to 1, then 7. The learner should notice that Massed is highest on day 1, but falls to 0% by day 30, while Expanding with Retrieval holds 65%. 5. The learner answers P3 and submits it. **Feedback:** P1 and P2 have one attempt each and are scored before the curves appear. P1 correct: "Yes — expanding gaps let each review come when the memory has faded a little, which strengthens it most." P1 incorrect, chose Massed: "Massed reviews come before any forgetting happens, so they add little lasting strength." P1 incorrect, chose Evenly spaced: "Close — spacing helps, but longer later gaps help more in this model." P1 incorrect, chose No review: "Without review, retention falls close to zero within a month." P2 correct: "Right — retrieval strengthens memory more than rereading." P2 incorrect: "Rereading feels effective, but recalling from memory builds more lasting strength." P3 has two attempts. P3 correct: "Yes — cramming wins tomorrow's test, which is why it feels like it works." P3 incorrect: "Look at the day-1 exam: the spaced reviews have not happened yet." After the second wrong attempt, the answer is shown. Score "n of 3" is shown at the end. **Starting State:** No curves are drawn. The four schedules are listed with their review days, and the prompt reads "Maya has three short reviews before a test on day 30. Which schedule, and which way of reviewing, will help her remember the most?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's worked example uses a test on day 30, three reviews, a cram plan on day 0, an evenly spaced plan on days 1, 3 and 7, and an expanding retrieval plan on days 1, 4 and 12. The chapter states that rereading gave better recall after five minutes and retrieval gave better recall after one week in Roediger and Karpicke (2006).
